# Degree of Accuracy for Multidimensional Gauss-Legendre Quadrature

## Setting Up the Problem

The 2D integral $\int_a^b \int_p^q f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$ is evaluated using a **tensor product** of 1D Gauss-Legendre rules:
$$\int_a^b \int_p^q f(x,y)\,dx\,dy \;\approx\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_i\,w_j\; f(x_i,\,y_j)$$
This uses $n$ points in the $x$-direction and $n$ points in the $y$-direction (total $n^2$ nodes).

## Degree of Precision in One Dimension

An $n$-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature is **exact** for every univariate polynomial up to degree
$$2n - 1$$
and **not** exact in general for degree $2n$.

## Extending to Two Dimensions (Tensor Product)

By the tensor product property, the 2D rule is exact for any polynomial $f(x,y)$ satisfying:
$$\deg_x f \le 2n-1 \quad \text{and} \quad \deg_y f \le 2n-1$$

That is, the rule integrates every monomial $x^i\,y^j$ exactly when
$$0 \le i \le 2n-1 \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \le j \le 2n-1.$$

## Identifying the Degree of Accuracy

The **degree of accuracy** (precision) of the quadrature rule is the highest polynomial degree for which the rule is exact in **each variable independently**. Since the 1D Gauss-Legendre rule with $n$ nodes achieves precision $2n-1$, and the tensor product preserves this bound in every coordinate direction, the multidimensional rule is exact for all polynomials of degree at most $2n-1$ in each variable.

**Verification with small $n$:**
| $n$ | 1D rule | Degree $2n-1$ | 2D tensor product |
|-----|---------|---------------|-------------------|
| 1 | Midpoint | 1 | Exact for $a+bx+cy+dxy$ ✓ |
| 2 | 2-pt Gauss | 3 | Exact up to $x^3y^3$ in each variable ✓ |

## Result

$$\boxed{2n-1}$$
